case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the ACA’s requirement that most private health plans cover certain evidence-based preventive services without cost-sharing is unconstitutional because the body that effectively sets many of those required services (the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force) is composed of members who were not appointed in conformity with the Appointments Clause (and relatedly, what the proper remedy should be).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. II, § 2, cl. 2 (Appointments Clause); Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act preventive-services coverage mandate, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a) (including the USPSTF-recommended services incorporated by reference in § 300gg-13(a)(1)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that the Fifth Circuit erred in concluding that the USPSTF’s role in the ACA preventive-services regime triggers an Appointments Clause violation warranting invalidation of the USPSTF-linked mandate. In the government’s view, USPSTF recommendations operate within a framework in which HHS has sufficient supervision/authority to satisfy Article II, and in any event the lower court’s remedy—setting aside the preventive-services requirements tied to USPSTF recommendations—was overbroad and destabilizing for nationwide preventive-care coverage. Petitioners emphasize the significant public-health, coverage, and systemic reliance interests supporting continued enforcement of no-cost preventive services.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that the ACA unlawfully delegates binding power to the USPSTF because, once the Task Force issues an “A” or “B” recommendation, insurers and group health plans become legally obligated to cover that service with no cost-sharing. Because USPSTF members are not Senate-confirmed officers, and respondents argue they are not appointed as constitutionally required for officials exercising significant federal authority, the preventive-services mandate is unconstitutional as applied to USPSTF-driven requirements. Respondents also raise justiciability/standing defenses to challenges against parts of the mandate not directly tied to their alleged injury and argue the proper remedy is to enjoin enforcement of the unconstitutional portions.
key_precedents: Weissman (D.C. Circuit purchaser-standing doctrine case referenced in the record excerpts)
Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s point about § 300gg-13(a)(1)’s automatic legal effect and Congress’s “independent” label is the hardest issue, because it resembles the unreviewable finality problem we addressed in Arthrex. But Edmond directs us to a functional inquiry—whether the work is directed and supervised “at some level” by a Senate-confirmed principal—and the Secretary’s at-will removal power and operational control within HHS supply that supervision even if Congress did not require a separate, contemporaneous “approval” step for each recommendation. Justice Alito is right that removal alone is not always sufficient, yet this scheme’s legal effect still runs through executive administration and enforcement, making it unlike a tribunal whose decisions are final within the Executive Branch absent principal-officer review. Even assuming some Article II tension, Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial logic counsels a narrow supervisory cure rather than the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping set-aside, and institutional legitimacy favors deciding no more than necessary to resolve this case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on at-will removal and general “administrative control” does not satisfy Edmond’s requirement that an inferior officer be directed and supervised in the exercise of the very power that has binding legal effect; here, § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations self-executing without any principal-officer review or reversal authority. Arthrex confirms the constitutional defect: the cure there was not mere removability but a mechanism for a Senate-confirmed officer to review and countermand decisions before they became final; nothing comparable exists for USPSTF recommendations “in effect.” Justice Kagan’s avoidance-based reconstruction lacks a textual foothold because Congress chose automatic incorporation and separately described the Task Force as “independent,” and my methodology does not permit rewriting a mandatory trigger into a discretionary approval regime. Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial tailoring cannot be used to preserve an arrangement that vests significant executive power in improperly appointed, unsupervised actors; the appropriate relief is to bar enforcement of the USPSTF-linked mandate absent constitutionally sufficient appointment and review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that at-will removal and HHS administrative control can satisfy Edmond’s “directed and supervised” standard, but Edmond and especially Arthrex focus on whether a principal officer can review and countermand the very decision that carries legal force. Here, § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes USPSTF “A”/“B” recommendations self-executing as coverage obligations for private plans, and the Secretary’s after-the-fact enforcement role is not the constitutionally relevant kind of review authority. Justice Kagan’s avoidance reading would effectively insert a Secretarial approval gate that Congress did not provide, and as a textualist I am unwilling to rewrite a mandatory incorporation (“in effect”) into a discretionary regime to save the statute. I agree with Justice Thomas that the statute’s “independent” design and the absence of a review mechanism at the moment of legal effect create an Appointments Clause problem, though the remedy should be tailored to the USPSTF-linked mandate consistent with Free Enterprise Fund’s severability principles.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the hardest point: § 300gg-13(a)(1) gives USPSTF “A”/“B” recommendations automatic legal consequence without an express Secretarial “approval” step, and the statute’s “independent” label seems to deny the kind of review emphasized in Edmond and Arthrex. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue, Edmond/Arthrex are functional: the question is whether a Senate-confirmed principal can meaningfully direct and supervise the relevant exercise of executive power, and here HHS’s enforcement/implementation machinery plus the Secretary’s at-will removal and operational control prevent the Task Force from wielding uncountermandable final Executive authority “on behalf of the United States.” Even assuming some Article II defect, Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial logic—also noted by Roberts—cuts strongly against the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping set-aside that would abruptly strip preventive-care protections from millions; the constitutionally appropriate response is a tailored supervision/appointment cure, not destabilizing nationwide access to care where narrower relief can vindicate Article II. Those doctrinal and real-world considerations together keep me with Petitioners.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is the self-executing nature of § 300gg-13(a)(1) coupled with Congress’s “independent” label, and Justice Alito reinforces that removal alone may not equal review in the Arthrex sense. But Edmond’s supervision inquiry is functional and looks to whether a Senate-confirmed principal can meaningfully direct and control the relevant executive work; here, as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the Secretary’s at-will removal authority plus HHS’s operational control and the Secretary’s control over enforcement/implementation keep the Task Force from wielding unreviewable final executive power. Arthrex matters, but it does not rigidly require a bespoke, on-the-record appellate review mechanism for every binding predicate; it requires that the Executive can ultimately control the legal consequences, and on a pragmatic, coherence-preserving reading the recommendations’ practical force still runs through HHS-administered machinery. Even assuming some Article II tension, I agree with Roberts and Kavanaugh that Free Enterprise Fund supports at most a narrow, prospective supervision/appointment cure rather than the Fifth Circuit’s destabilizing set-aside, so I remain with Petitioner on avoidance and remedy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is structural: § 300gg-13(a)(1) attaches legal consequences to USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations without an express Secretarial sign-off, and § 299b-4(a)(6)’s “independent” label underscores that concern. But as the Chief Justice stresses, Edmond asks whether the work is “directed and supervised at some level” by a Senate-confirmed principal, and the Secretary’s at-will removal authority plus operational control over the Task Force’s placement and implementation within HHS are meaningful supervisory tools that keep these members in the inferior-officer lane. Justice Alito is right that Arthrex looked for review of decisions with binding effect, yet here the legal obligation still runs through the Executive’s administration and enforcement machinery rather than through self-executing adjudications by the Task Force itself, making the absence of a formal review step less dispositive on a textual and original understanding of Article II supervision. Even if one thought the statutory scheme creates a constitutional defect, Free Enterprise Fund supports a narrow, supervision-restoring remedy rather than the Fifth Circuit’s broad set-aside.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best point that § 300gg-13(a)(1) gives USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations automatic downstream legal effect without an express Secretarial “approval” step, which can resemble the unreviewable finality problem in Arthrex. But under Edmond and Arthrex, the constitutional touchstone is practical direction and supervision by a Senate-confirmed principal, and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that at-will removal plus HHS’s structural and implementation control over the Task Force’s work and enforcement of the mandate supply meaningful executive accountability notwithstanding the statutory label “independent.” Even if one perceived a defect, Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial principles—emphasized by Roberts—support a narrow, supervision-restoring prospective fix rather than the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping set-aside that would destabilize entrenched reliance interests absent a clear, unavoidable Article II violation. On an institutionalist, precedent-focused approach, the better course is to reverse (or at most remand for a tailored remedy), not invalidate nationwide preventive-services coverage based on a formalistic reading that ignores functional supervision.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best objection: § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations self-executing, and the statute’s “independent” label suggests the Secretary cannot review the very act that creates legal effect. But Edmond and Arthrex ask a functional supervision question—whether a Senate-confirmed principal can direct and supervise the relevant exercise of authority—not whether Congress inserted an express “approval” checkpoint, and the Secretary’s at-will removal power plus HHS’s operational control over the Task Force’s placement and support are substantial supervisory tools even if the recommendations are incorporated by reference. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts that, if any Appointments Clause tension remains, Free Enterprise Fund points toward a narrow, supervision-restoring remedy rather than the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping set-aside of the preventive-services mandate. On a textualist/originalist approach, I am reluctant to treat “independent” as creating constitutionally unreviewable executive power when the broader statutory and administrative scheme supplies meaningful principal-officer control.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best contrary point: § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes USPSTF “A”/“B” recommendations self-executing, and “independent” in § 299b-4(a)(6) suggests no Article II supervision at the moment legal consequences attach. But under Edmond and Arthrex, the constitutional inquiry is functional—whether a Senate-confirmed principal can direct and supervise the exercise of authority—and I find Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the Secretary’s at-will removal and HHS’s operational control, coupled with the fact that HHS administers and enforces the mandate, sufficient to prevent these recommendations from being “final” executive decisions in the Arthrex sense. Even if there is constitutional tension in the statute’s incorporation mechanism, Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial principles (as Roberts and Justice Sotomayor note) require a narrow, supervision-restoring fix rather than the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping set-aside that disregards reliance interests and workable governance. On my pragmatic, fairness-oriented approach, we should avoid destabilizing nationwide preventive-care obligations when the constitutional concern can be addressed through a tailored prospective remedy (or a supervision-preserving construction).

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Edmond v. United States, inferior officers are those “whose work is directed and supervised at some level by” a Senate-confirmed principal officer, and the relevant question is how much authority they exercise free from such control. Here, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations, but the Secretary of HHS—acting through AHRQ—possesses meaningful supervisory tools (including at-will removal and administrative control over the Task Force’s operations), which weighs against treating Task Force members as unsupervised principal officers under Edmond and Arthrex. Even if some Appointments Clause defect existed, institutional and reliance interests counsel a narrow remedy rather than setting aside the USPSTF-linked mandate wholesale, consistent with this Court’s approach in Free Enterprise Fund to tailor relief to the constitutional violation. Given the ACA’s nationwide reliance and the availability of supervision-based narrowing constructions, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit’s broad invalidation and rule for the government on the narrowest grounds possible.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Appointments Clause requires that officers exercising “significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States” be appointed in the constitutionally prescribed manner, Buckley v. Valeo, and the ACA makes USPSTF “A” or “B” recommendations legally binding by incorporating them into § 300gg-13(a)(1)’s coverage mandate. Under Edmond v. United States, inferior officers must be “directed and supervised at some level” by Senate-confirmed superiors; here, the statute characterizes the Task Force as “independent,” 42 U.S.C. § 299b-4(a)(6), and provides only administrative support rather than meaningful review or supervision, so its members cannot constitutionally wield final, binding regulatory power without proper appointment. Consistent with Lucia v. SEC and Free Enterprise Fund, the proper remedy is to set aside or enjoin enforcement of the USPSTF-linked requirements unless and until Congress or the Executive supplies constitutionally adequate appointment and supervision, rather than allowing an unconstitutional structure to continue operating. The government’s policy and reliance arguments cannot override the Constitution’s text and original separation-of-powers design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 300gg-13(a)(1) gives legally binding effect to USPSTF “A” or “B” recommendations by automatically imposing a no-cost-coverage obligation on private plans, a hallmark of “significant authority” that must be exercised by properly appointed Officers under Article II. Under Edmond v. United States, an officer is “inferior” only if his work is directed and supervised at some level by Senate-confirmed superiors, and the practical structure here—where recommendations become mandatory without a contemporaneous, discretionary Secretarial approval—provides insufficient supervision and direction. Consistent with Buckley v. Valeo and Lucia v. SEC, the Constitution does not permit Congress to vest rule-like power in a body whose members were not appointed in conformity with the Appointments Clause. The remedy should be tailored to the USPSTF-linked portion of § 300gg-13(a)(1), rather than unsettling the entire preventive-services regime, in line with Free Enterprise Fund’s remedial approach favoring narrower invalidation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations into coverage obligations, but the Appointments Clause question turns on whether Task Force members exercise unreviewable final executive power or instead operate under sufficient direction and supervision by a Senate-confirmed principal officer. Under Edmond v. United States and this Court’s emphasis on whether an officer can render a final decision “on behalf of the United States” without review, the Secretary’s at-will removal authority and capacity to supervise, channel, and ultimately control the incorporation and administration of recommendations weigh strongly against treating USPSTF members as unconstrained principal officers. Even if some constitutional defect existed, the Fifth Circuit’s sweeping remedy—setting aside nationwide preventive-services requirements tied to USPSTF recommendations—disregards reliance interests and access-to-care consequences for vulnerable populations, and runs counter to the Court’s usual preference for narrower, remedial tailoring (e.g., Free Enterprise Fund). The better course is to uphold the mandate or, at most, adopt a limited remedy that cures any supervision problem without destabilizing preventive-care coverage under the ACA.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations into an HHS-administered insurance-coverage regime, and the better reading—consistent with statutory coherence and constitutional avoidance—is that the Secretary retains sufficient direction-and-supervision authority over whether and how those recommendations operate as binding legal obligations. Under Edmond v. United States, the hallmark of an inferior officer is being “directed and supervised” by a Senate-confirmed principal; here the preventive-services mandate functions within HHS’s enforcement and regulatory apparatus, making nationwide invalidation of USPSTF-linked requirements an overbroad, destabilizing remedy inconsistent with Free Enterprise Fund’s preference for narrower cures. Even assuming an Appointments Clause problem, Lucia and Ryder indicate the ordinary fix is a prospective, properly appointed decisionmaker rather than sweeping disruption of settled regulatory reliance interests. Given the ACA’s structure and purpose to ensure workable, evidence-based preventive coverage, the Fifth Circuit’s remedy goes too far.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Appointments Clause turns on whether the officials exercise significant federal authority free from sufficient supervision, and inferior officers are those “whose work is directed and supervised at some level” by a principal officer. Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663 (1997). Here, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations, but the better reading—consistent with Edmond and this Court’s focus on control in Arthrex—is that Task Force members do not render final, unreviewable decisions on behalf of the United States where the Secretary retains ultimate supervisory tools (including at-will removal and the Department’s capacity to manage implementation). Even assuming some structural defect, separation-of-powers remedies should be tailored (Free Enterprise Fund), making the Fifth Circuit’s broad setting-aside of the USPSTF-linked coverage requirements an overcorrection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Edmond v. United States, inferior officers are those whose work is “directed and supervised at some level” by Senate-confirmed principal officers, and that supervision is typically satisfied where a principal can remove at will and control whether the subordinate’s actions have binding legal effect. Here, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF recommendations into coverage requirements, but the better reading—consistent with Article II avoidance and practical workability—recognizes the Secretary of HHS’s overarching supervisory authority and removal power as sufficient to render Task Force members inferior officers. In line with Free Enterprise Fund and Lucia, even if there were a defect, the remedy should be tailored rather than the Fifth Circuit’s broad “set aside” approach that would destabilize nationwide preventive-services coverage and upset substantial reliance interests. Judicial restraint and the Court’s institutional role favor upholding the regime or, at most, adopting a narrower prospective remedy tied to supervision rather than invalidating the mandate wholesale.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 300gg-13(a)(1) incorporates USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations into the preventive-services mandate, but under Edmond v. United States an officer is “inferior” when his work is directed and supervised at some level by a principal officer, and the Secretary of HHS retains substantial supervisory tools. In particular, the Secretary’s at-will removal authority and ability to control whether and how recommendations become operative within HHS’s administration of the ACA are the kind of direction-and-supervision features that, under Edmond and Arthrex, prevent the Task Force from exercising unreviewable final executive power. Even if some aspect of the statutory scheme were read to give USPSTF recommendations binding effect without adequate executive control, precedent favors a narrower, severability-focused remedy rather than wholesale invalidation of the USPSTF-linked mandate. Accordingly, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit’s Appointments Clause holding and reject its overbroad remedy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Appointments Clause problem is substantially mitigated if USPSTF members function as inferior officers whose work is "directed and supervised" by a principal officer, Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663 (1997), and the statutory scheme can be read to preserve meaningful HHS oversight over whether and how recommendations translate into enforceable coverage obligations under 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a)(1). Even assuming a constitutional defect in the way USPSTF recommendations are incorporated, the Fifth Circuit’s broad remedy of setting aside USPSTF-linked preventive-services requirements is inconsistent with this Court’s usual approach of tailoring relief to the violation and respecting reliance interests, see Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010). Given the practical consequences for nationwide preventive-care access and the availability of narrower severability/administrative fixes, I would not invalidate the mandate as applied across the board. Procedural fairness and stability favor sustaining the framework or, at most, remanding for a limited remedy that cures any supervision/appointment deficiency without disrupting existing coverage.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Affordable Care Act’s preventive-services coverage mandate is unconstitutional or otherwise unlawful because it incorporates recommendations of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (and related expert bodies) whose members were not appointed in conformity with the Appointments Clause, and whether plaintiffs have standing and viable RFRA objections to specific required coverages such as PrEP.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. II, § 2, cl. 2 (Appointments Clause); Affordable Care Act § 2713, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13 (coverage of preventive health services); Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), 42 U.S.C. § 2000bb et seq. (as applied to the PrEP coverage requirement).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The federal government argues that the ACA’s preventive-services framework is lawful and administrable: the Task Force and other expert bodies function as advisory entities whose recommendations may be adopted through lawful executive implementation, and in any event any Appointments Clause concern can be cured through severability or proper supervision rather than invalidating the mandate wholesale. The government and supporting amici also contend that the Fifth Circuit’s approach would destabilize a major component of the ACA that ensures no-cost coverage for widely used, evidence-based preventive care, and that respondents’ challenges (including RFRA-based objections tied to PrEP) fail on threshold grounds like standing/ripeness and on the merits because the mandate serves compelling public health interests through the least restrictive means.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that § 2713 unlawfully delegates binding federal power to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and similar bodies, because their recommendations effectively become mandatory coverage requirements without the members being appointed as constitutionally valid 'Officers of the United States' or being adequately supervised by Senate-confirmed officials; thus the preventive-services mandate is unconstitutional under the Appointments Clause and must be set aside (at least as to the Task Force-driven requirements). Respondents also argue they have standing because the law imposes a present legal obligation that affects plan design and exposes them to compliance costs and enforcement risk, and that RFRA independently prohibits forcing them to provide coverage for PrEP, which they characterize as facilitating conduct conflicting with their religious beliefs.
key_precedents: Weissman (D.C. Circuit purchaser-standing doctrine referenced in the record excerpts)
Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) line of cases (generally implicated by the PrEP objection, though not specifically named in the provided excerpts)
Appointments Clause doctrine (generally implicated; no specific Supreme Court case names are provided in the excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s textual point is the hardest: § 300gg-13(a)(1) keys a coverage duty to USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations without an express “as adopted by the Secretary” clause, and Arthrex cautions that removal or generalized implementation is not the same as review. But I do not read the statute to make the Task Force’s ratings legally self-executing in the Article II sense; as Justice Kagan emphasizes, these are “recommendations” operating within an enforcement and administration scheme in which a Senate-confirmed Secretary must implement, take responsibility for, and can prospectively control what becomes binding in practice—bringing the case within Edmond’s supervision framework rather than Buckley/Lucia’s freestanding exercise of final federal power. Constitutional avoidance and institutional legitimacy counsel a narrow construction (and, if necessary, a targeted forward-looking supervisory remedy) rather than setting aside the USPSTF pathway wholesale on a reading that treats an advisory body as an unaccountable lawmaker. I agree with Justice Thomas that we cannot invent authority, but here the statute’s operation through HHS administration provides a fair, minimal-disruption basis to require accountable Secretarial control at the point recommendations acquire binding effect.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s Edmond/avoidance approach is the strongest counterargument, but it still depends on locating in § 300gg-13(a)(1) a Secretarial adoption, ratification, or review mechanism that the text does not supply; Congress made plans’ duties turn on USPSTF “A” or “B” recommendations, not on recommendations as the Secretary approves. As Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Arthrex teaches that at-will removal and generalized “implementation” authority are not meaningful review of a decision that has binding legal effect, and Edmond’s inferior-officer framework helps only where the superior can actually direct and countermand the operative determination. Buckley and Lucia therefore remain controlling on the point that this kind of binding effect is “significant authority,” and constitutional avoidance cannot be used to rewrite the statutory trigger to create accountability that Congress did not enact. The appropriate course is targeted relief from USPSTF-driven mandates unless and until Congress provides constitutionally adequate supervision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Edmond/avoidance approach is the most serious counterargument, but it still relies on implying a Secretarial adoption/ratification mechanism that § 300gg-13(a)(1) does not supply; the statute makes the coverage duty turn on current USPSTF “A” or “B” recommendations, not on recommendations as approved by the Secretary. Justice Kagan’s point that “recommendations” operate within an implementation scheme cannot overcome Arthrex’s insistence that removal and general administrative authority are not meaningful review where an actor’s decision has automatic legal effect. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed supervisory “fix” likewise presupposes authority to review and countermand that the text does not confer, and avoidance does not permit us to add that missing step. The appropriate course is a narrow remedy limited to the USPSTF-triggered mandates, preserving the remainder while restoring Article II accountability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: § 300gg-13(a)(1) keys mandatory coverage to USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations without an express “as adopted by the Secretary” clause, and Arthrex makes clear that removal power is not equivalent to review of decisions with binding legal effect. But I remain persuaded by the Chief Justice’s Edmond-based framing that the constitutional question is whether a Senate-confirmed official can meaningfully supervise and take responsibility for what becomes legally operative, and—consistent with Justice Kagan’s view—the ACA’s enforcement and administrative machinery can and should be read to require accountable Secretarial implementation/ratification before those recommendations bind regulated parties. That reading is not a freewheeling rewrite so much as a constitutional-avoidance construction of how “recommendations” acquire legal force in an executive program; and if current practice has treated them as self-executing, the Arthrex-compliant remedy is a narrow supervisory fix, not a disruptive set-aside that predictably harms access to no-cost preventive care for those least able to pay. No colleague has shown that the statute unmistakably forecloses any such accountable mediation at the point of enforcement, so the respondents’ textual argument does not genuinely undermine my approach.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: § 300gg-13(a)(1) does not say “as adopted by the Secretary,” and if USPSTF “A”/“B” ratings are legally self-executing, Arthrex and Lucia make the Appointments Clause problem serious. But I think Chief Justice Roberts is right to reframe the inquiry under Edmond: the statute’s use of “recommendations,” placed within an HHS-administered and HHS-enforced coverage regime, is most coherently read to require Secretarial implementation that supplies accountable adoption/ratification and ongoing supervisory control over what becomes binding law—an interpretation that fits ordinary administrative practice rather than rewriting the trigger. Justice Thomas is right to warn that avoidance cannot invent a veto power out of thin air, yet the better textual reading is that “recommendations” do not themselves impose enforceable duties absent the Secretary’s legally operative incorporation into the regulatory/enforcement system. Even if current practice has treated USPSTF output as effectively automatic, the remedy should be targeted (as Roberts/Kavanaugh suggest) to ensure meaningful principal-officer review going forward, not facial invalidation of the preventive-services framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Edmond/avoidance argument is the best case for Petitioners, but as Justice Barrett emphasizes, § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes the legal duty turn on services “recommended” with an “A” or “B” rating—without any textual adoption, ratification, or veto step by a Senate-confirmed officer. Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right that “recommendations” operate within an implementation and enforcement scheme, yet Arthrex teaches that enforcement discretion or at-will removal is not the constitutionally relevant supervisory power where the operative decision’s legal effect is set by someone other than a principal officer. Edmond helps only if there is a lawful mechanism for a superior to direct and revise the decision that triggers binding obligations, and I do not see such a mechanism in the statutory trigger as written; avoidance cannot supply what Congress omitted. The narrow remedy remains to set aside only the USPSTF-driven mandates while leaving Congress free to install constitutionally adequate review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch have the strongest textual point: § 300gg-13(a)(1) does not expressly say “as adopted by the Secretary,” so treating USPSTF ratings as automatically binding creates a serious Arthrex/Lucia problem if no principal officer can countermand the operative decision. But Chief Justice Roberts’s Edmond framing is still persuasive to me because the statute’s trigger—“recommendations”—operates within an executive enforcement and implementation regime in which a Senate-confirmed Secretary can be required to take responsibility for what becomes legally obligatory, and constitutional avoidance counsels adopting that accountability-preserving construction rather than the most constitutionally fraught reading. Justice Thomas is right that removal alone is not “review,” which is why the appropriate remedy is an Arthrex-style supervisory cure (clear Secretarial ratification/review going forward) rather than setting aside the USPSTF pathway wholesale. Given the reliance interests and the availability of a narrower fix consistent with severability and institutional legitimacy, I do not think the respondents’ textual objection compels invalidation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s avoidance construction is the strongest counter: that “recommendations” must be mediated through Secretarial implementation, permitting adoption/ratification and thus Edmond-style supervision. But the enacted trigger in § 300gg-13(a)(1) makes coverage turn on services “recommended” by the USPSTF with an “A” or “B” rating, without any textual hook for a principal officer to approve, revise, or countermand the operative rating before it binds regulated parties; reading such a step in supplies authority Congress did not confer. Arthrex reinforces that removal or generalized enforcement discretion cannot substitute for a superior’s review power over the decision that carries legal effect, so Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “implementation” accounts do not cure the Article II defect on the statute’s terms. The appropriate course is therefore a narrow remedy directed to USPSTF-driven mandates unless and until constitutionally adequate supervision is provided, consistent with severability and minimal necessary relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch are right to press that § 300gg-13(a)(1) keys coverage to USPSTF “A”/“B” recommendations and that Arthrex demands more than at-will removal when a decision is effectively final. But I do not read the statute as making USPSTF outputs self-executing federal law in the absence of Secretarial implementation within the ACA’s enforcement and rulemaking architecture, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize; the legal obligation becomes concrete through HHS’s accountable administration, guidance, and enforcement choices. Justice Thomas’s warning that avoidance cannot relabel binding mandates as “advisory” is an important constraint, yet it supports (in my view) a narrow, procedurally regular remedy: require Secretarial adoption/ratification or comparable review at the point where obligations are made enforceable, rather than a broad set-aside that would upend settled reliance interests in no-cost preventive care. That approach preserves Article II accountability consistent with Edmond while minimizing disruption and respecting severability principles.

John Roberts.reasoning: A narrow resolution is available that avoids destabilizing 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13 while addressing any Appointments Clause concerns: under Edmond v. United States, Task Force members may be treated as inferior officers so long as their work is directed and supervised at some level by a Senate-confirmed principal officer, with removal and meaningful oversight as key tools of control. If the statutory scheme can be construed or implemented to ensure Secretarial supervision and review sufficient to cure any constitutional defect, that construction is preferable to invalidating the preventive-services mandate wholesale, consistent with institutional legitimacy and severability principles. On the RFRA/PrEP challenge, relief—if any—should be confined to the particular plaintiffs and coverage at issue, and only upon a concrete showing of standing and a substantial burden under RFRA, rather than a broad facial set-aside of § 2713.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Appointments Clause requires that any person exercising “significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States” be appointed as an “Officer of the United States” in the manner Article II prescribes. Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, 126 (1976). Section 2713, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13, makes the Task Force’s preventive-services recommendations legally binding coverage mandates; if those mandates flow automatically from the Task Force’s determinations, then Task Force members wield significant federal power without constitutionally valid appointment or adequate supervision. Because respondents face a present legal obligation affecting plan design and compliance costs, they have standing to challenge the mandate, and any RFRA claim as to PrEP is at least viable insofar as the government has not shown the requirement is applied through the least restrictive means under 42 U.S.C. § 2000bb-1.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2713, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13, as implemented, appears to give U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations binding legal effect (mandatory no-cost coverage) without those decisionmakers being appointed or supervised in a manner consistent with Article II’s Appointments Clause. Under Lucia v. SEC, officials exercising continuing “significant authority” are Officers, and under Edmond v. United States and Arthrex the Constitution requires a clear chain of command and meaningful superior control over final federal decisions; that accountability is difficult to square with an expert body whose determinations effectively dictate private parties’ legal obligations. Respondents plausibly have standing because the mandate imposes present compliance duties and costs on plan design, and at least as to PrEP, RFRA (42 U.S.C. § 2000bb et seq.) can bar compelled coverage that substantially burdens religious exercise absent a demonstrated least-restrictive-means justification. Given the practical consequences and the availability of narrower remedies (e.g., invalidating only the Task Force-driven mandates), the constitutional defect should be addressed rather than waved away as merely “advisory.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2713’s preventive-services regime can be administered consistently with the Appointments Clause because the Task Force’s recommendations become binding only through executive implementation and supervision, and the Secretary’s at-will removal power and ability to control whether recommendations take effect are hallmarks of an “inferior officer” relationship rather than unsupervised final decisionmaking. Under Lucia v. SEC, the relevant inquiry is whether the officials exercise “significant authority” with final effect; here, the government’s account of secretarial oversight and ratification materially distinguishes this scheme from one in which nonappointed actors issue final, unreviewable rules. Even if some aspect of § 300gg-13 were read to insufficiently cabin the Task Force, the appropriate remedy would be severing any undue insulation and preserving the preventive-care mandate’s core, given the destabilizing real-world consequences for access to no-cost preventive care. Plaintiffs’ RFRA challenge to PrEP should not justify sweeping relief absent a concrete, traceable injury and, in any event, the mandate serves compelling public-health interests through a generally applicable coverage rule rather than targeting religious exercise.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2713’s text is best read, consistent with statutory coherence and workability, to operate through the Secretary’s implementation authority rather than to confer unsupervised, binding federal power on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force; that construction avoids an Appointments Clause problem while keeping the preventive-services scheme administrable. Under Lucia v. SEC, an entity becomes an “Officer[] of the United States” when it exercises continuing “significant authority,” but where a Senate-confirmed department head retains ultimate control—through adoption, supervision, or ratification of what would otherwise be advisory recommendations—the chain-of-command accountability demanded by Free Enterprise Fund and Arthrex is satisfied. Even if any portion of the Task Force pathway were constitutionally problematic, the appropriate remedy is a targeted fix (severability/valid adoption by a properly accountable official), not wholesale invalidation of § 2713’s preventive-coverage regime. Plaintiffs’ RFRA objection to PrEP, on this record, is better addressed as an as-applied claim requiring a concrete showing of substantial burden and least-restrictive-means analysis, rather than a basis to dismantle the broader mandate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2713 makes USPSTF “A” and “B” recommendations legally binding coverage mandates on private parties, so Task Force members wield “significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States” and thus are “Officers” under Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, 126 (1976). Because those officers were not appointed in conformity with Article II, § 2, cl. 2, and because the statute does not clearly provide constitutionally adequate supervision by a Senate-confirmed principal officer over the binding recommendations, the mandate is unconstitutional as applied to those recommendations. Separation-of-powers principles counsel against sustaining a regime where unsupervised, non–Senate-confirmed actors effectively write binding federal law; any “saving construction” must be rooted in the text (42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13(a)(1)) and cannot rewrite Congress’s chosen mechanism. Given a present legal obligation affecting plan design and compliance costs, plaintiffs have standing, and their RFRA challenge to PrEP at least warrants merits consideration rather than dismissal on threshold grounds.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651 (1997), an official’s status as an “inferior Officer” turns principally on whether the work is “directed and supervised” by Senate-confirmed officers; here, § 2713’s use of “recommendations” is best read to preserve the HHS Secretary’s ultimate supervisory authority over whether and how preventive-services guidance is implemented, which avoids converting the USPSTF into an unsupervised lawmaking body. Applying constitutional-avoidance and severability principles (see Free Enter. Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)), any Appointments Clause defect should be cured by ensuring appropriate Secretarial supervision rather than invalidating the preventive-services mandate wholesale, given the statute’s workability and reliance interests. On the record described, respondents’ RFRA challenge to PrEP is also doubtful on threshold justiciability and merits because the mandate serves compelling public-health interests and the remedy should be narrowly tailored to any proven substantial burden. Respect for precedent, practical consequences, and institutional stability favors reversing the Fifth Circuit’s destabilizing approach and upholding the framework as lawfully administered under 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2713, 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13, makes certain USPSTF recommendations binding on private plans without a clear mechanism for review or adoption by a Senate-confirmed official, suggesting the Task Force members exercise continuing “significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States” and thus implicate the Appointments Clause. Under Lucia v. SEC and Arthrex, the constitutional problem is not merely advisory input but final, unreviewable effect; absent a “clear and effective chain of command” to a properly appointed superior, the mandate as to USPSTF-triggered services is unlawful. Given that respondents face present compliance obligations and attendant costs, standing is satisfied, and any RFRA objection to particular coverages (e.g., PrEP) is at least viable for individualized adjudication rather than categorical dismissal. The appropriate remedy follows Appointments Clause doctrine emphasizing that actions by improperly appointed officers are infirm, favoring setting aside the USPSTF-driven requirements unless and until lawfully supervised or reconstituted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because § 2713’s preventive-services regime can be administered consistent with Article II through lawful supervision and ratification by a Senate-confirmed official, I would not invalidate the mandate wholesale on an Appointments Clause theory. Under Buckley v. Valeo and Lucia v. SEC, actors exercising “significant authority” may be “Officers,” but the appropriate remedy is to ensure constitutionally accountable control (including ratification or corrective supervision), not to unwind widely relied-upon, evidence-based coverage requirements where narrower relief will cure any defect. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against disruptive, across-the-board vacatur when severability and executive oversight can address the constitutional concern while preserving access to no-cost preventive care under 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-13. As to RFRA, plaintiffs must show a concrete, traceable injury and a substantial burden tied to particular coverage requirements; generalized objections to PrEP coverage should be evaluated with careful attention to standing and to the government’s compelling public-health interests under RFRA’s least-restrictive-means test.
